s0003.literal: Prince of Shixing Chen Shuling; Prince of Xin'an Chen Bogu
s0003.idiomatic: Prince of Shixing Chen Shuling; Prince of Xin'an Chen Bogu

s0005.literal: Prince of Shixing Chen Shuling, styled Zisong, was the second son of Emperor Gaozong.
s0005.idiomatic: Prince of Shixing Chen Shuling, styled Zisong, was Emperor Gaozong's second son.

s0006.literal: In the Chengsheng era of Liang, Emperor Gaozong was at Jiangling as direct-gate general, and Shuling was born there.
s0006.idiomatic: During Liang's Chengsheng reign, Emperor Gaozong was at Jiangling as direct-gate general when Shuling was born.

s0007.literal: When Jiangling fell, Emperor Gaozong removed to Guanzhong; Shuling remained at Rangcheng.
s0007.idiomatic: After Jiangling fell, Emperor Gaozong withdrew to Guanzhong while Shuling stayed behind at Rangcheng.

s0008.literal: When Emperor Gaozong returned, the Last Ruler and Shuling were left as hostages.
s0008.idiomatic: On Emperor Gaozong's return, the Last Ruler and Shuling were held as hostages.

s0009.literal: In the third year of Tianchen, he followed the Last Ruler back to court, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Kangle with a fief of five hundred households.
s0009.idiomatic: In Tianchen year 3 he followed the Last Ruler home to court and was made Marquis of Kangle with a fief of five hundred households.

s0010.literal: Shuling in youth was quick-witted and disputatious, pursued reputation, and was overbearing—none could make him yield.
s0010.idiomatic: As a youth Shuling was sharp and argumentative, hungry for fame, and so overbearing that no one could stand up to him.

s0011.literal: In the first year of Guangda, he was appointed vice director of the Secretariat.
s0011.idiomatic: In Guangda year 1 he was made vice director of the Secretariat.

s0012.literal: In the second year, he went out as credential-bearing, commander of all military affairs in Jiang province, southern central-guard general, and inspector of Jiang.
s0012.idiomatic: In year 2 he went out bearing the staff, as commander of Jiang military affairs, southern central-guard general, and inspector of Jiang.

s0013.literal: In the first year of Taijian, he was enfeoffed as Prince of Shixing to maintain the cult of Prince Zhaolie.
s0013.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 he was made Prince of Shixing to carry on the sacrifices to Prince Zhaolie.

s0014.literal: He was further given the credential staff, command of all military affairs in Jiang, Ying, and Jin provinces, and the post of army mentor general; his inspectorate was unchanged.
s0014.idiomatic: He was further granted the credential staff, command over Jiang, Ying, and Jin, and the rank of army mentor general while keeping the inspectorate.

s0015.literal: Shuling was then sixteen; government issued from himself alone, and his staff had no part in it.
s0015.idiomatic: Shuling was then sixteen; policy came only from him, and his aides were shut out.

s0016.literal: By nature he was harsh and severe; his subordinates were awed and fearful.
s0016.idiomatic: He was harsh by nature, and his subordinates lived in dread.

s0017.literal: The various princes' sons and nephews and dismissed county magistrates and prefects were all forced to serve him.
s0017.idiomatic: Imperial nephews and dismissed county and prefectural heads alike were forced into his service.

s0018.literal: Yuzhang inner administrator Qian Facheng came to the mansion to pay his respects; Shuling at once assigned Facheng's son Jiqing to lead horse equipage; Jiqing, ashamed, did not come in good time; Shuling in great anger insulted and humiliated Facheng, and Facheng in resentment and grievance hanged himself and died.
s0018.idiomatic: When Yuzhang inner administrator Qian Facheng came to the princely residence to pay court, Shuling immediately detailed Facheng's son Jiqing to lead horse and arms. Jiqing, mortified, delayed; Shuling flew into a rage and abused Facheng until Facheng, bitter and aggrieved, hanged himself.

s0019.literal: Counties and prefectures outside his jurisdiction he also summoned and tried; court nobles and lower officials who crossed him he at once falsely memorialized for crimes and trapped them in capital punishment.
s0019.idiomatic: He even hauled in and prosecuted counties and prefectures outside his command; any court noble or petty official who offended him he would falsely denounce and trap in a capital sentence.

s0020.literal: Soon he was advanced in rank to cloud-banner general and given the additional post of scattered-cavalry regular attendant.
s0020.idiomatic: Soon he was promoted to cloud-banner general with the added title of scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0021.literal: In the third year, he was given the additional post of palace attendant.
s0021.idiomatic: In year 3 he was also made palace attendant.

s0022.literal: In the fourth year, he was transferred to command all military affairs in Xiang, Heng, Gui, and Wu provinces, made general who pacifies the south and inspector of Xiang; palace attendant and credential staff were unchanged.
s0022.idiomatic: In year 4 he was moved to command Xiang, Heng, Gui, and Wu, made general who pacifies the south and inspector of Xiang, while retaining palace attendant and the credential staff.

s0023.literal: When the garrisons of the provinces heard he was coming, all trembled in terror, their legs shaking.
s0023.idiomatic: Garrisons throughout the provinces shook with terror when they heard he was coming.

s0024.literal: Shuling daily grew more violent and overbearing; in campaigns against the Yi tribesmen everything taken went into his own purse—he never rewarded with the slightest share.
s0024.idiomatic: Shuling grew daily more brutal; on campaigns against the Yi he kept every prize for himself and never gave the least reward.

s0025.literal: His levies for labor and service had no limit or end.
s0025.idiomatic: His demands for labor and corvée knew no bounds.

s0026.literal: At night he often did not lie down; he burned candles until dawn, summoned guests, and spoke of petty matters among the people—jest and banter of every sort.
s0026.idiomatic: He seldom slept at night, kept candles burning till dawn, called in guests, and gossiped over village trifles, joking without restraint.

s0027.literal: By nature he did not drink wine; he only set out many dishes of meat and ate and gnawed day and night.
s0027.idiomatic: He did not drink, but heaped the table with meats and ate constantly, day and night.

s0028.literal: Only from dawn to midday did he finally sleep.
s0028.idiomatic: Only from morning till noon did he finally sleep.

s0029.literal: Documents in his offices—unless summoned, clerks might not present them on their own.
s0029.idiomatic: Office papers might not be submitted unless he called for them.

s0030.literal: Those flogged for punishment were all imprisoned; for years on end he often did not look in on them.
s0030.idiomatic: Anyone flogged was thrown into prison and often left unvisited for years.

s0031.literal: South of the Xiao and Xiang, he forced all into his personal service; in hamlet after hamlet almost none were left.
s0031.idiomatic: South of the Xiao and Xiang he pressed everyone into personal service until the hamlets were nearly emptied.

s0032.literal: If among them any escaped, he at once killed their wives and children.
s0032.idiomatic: Any who escaped he killed along with their wives and children.

s0033.literal: The prefectures and counties dared not report upward; Emperor Gaozong did not know of it.
s0033.idiomatic: Local officials dared not report up the chain, and Emperor Gaozong never learned of it.

s0034.literal: Soon he was advanced to general who guards the south and given a set of martial pipes and drums; he was moved to central guard general.
s0034.idiomatic: Soon he was promoted to general who guards the south with a suite of pipes and drums and transferred to central guard general.

s0035.literal: In the ninth year, he was appointed credential-bearing, commander of all military affairs in Yang, Xu, Eastern Yang, and Southern Yu provinces, and inspector of Yang; palace attendant, general, and pipes and drums were unchanged.
s0035.idiomatic: In year 9 he received the credential staff, command of Yang, Xu, Eastern Yang, and Southern Yu, and the Yangzhou inspectorate, while keeping palace attendant, his general's rank, and the pipes and drums.

s0036.literal: In the tenth year he reached the capital; he was given bearers and an oil-canopy carriage.
s0036.idiomatic: In year 10 he arrived at the capital and was granted sedan bearers and an oil-canopy carriage.

s0037.literal: Shuling's administration was at the Eastern Mansion; many affairs passed through the provincial offices. The bureaus in charge, if they followed his intent and bent to his will, he would hint to the throne to employ them; the slightest opposition he would strike with a great crime—the serious cases reaching execution by dismemberment. On the roads the talk was loud that he harbored extraordinary designs.
s0037.idiomatic: Shuling governed from the Eastern Mansion and routed much business through the provincial ministries. Offices that flattered him he pushed for imperial appointment; the least resistance brought a capital charge, even dismemberment. Rumors on every road said he nursed treasonous ambition.

s0038.literal: Shuling cultivated a false reputation; whenever he entered court he would in carriage or on horseback hold a scroll and read aloud, reciting in a loud voice, composed and self-satisfied.
s0038.idiomatic: Shuling cultivated a false reputation; entering court he would read aloud from a scroll in his carriage or on his horse, declaiming loudly with an air of ease.

s0039.literal: Back in his study he would sometimes himself take hatchet and adze to perform monkey masquerades.
s0039.idiomatic: Back in his study he sometimes took up hatchet and adze to play the monkey masquerader.

s0040.literal: He also loved to roam among tombs; when he met a mound whose occupant's name could be read on the tablet, he would order his attendants to dig it up, take the stone epitaph and ancient vessels, and even the bones of arm and shin, which he kept as playthings stored in his treasury.
s0040.idiomatic: He loved wandering graveyards; whenever a tombstone gave a readable name he had attendants open the mound, seize stone epitaphs and antiquities, even arm and shin bones, and kept them as toys in his storehouse.

s0041.literal: Among the people within the mansion, young wives and maidens of even slight beauty he at once forced into his harem.
s0041.idiomatic: Within the mansion he forced every young wife or maiden of even slight beauty into his bed.

s0042.literal: In the eleventh year he left office in mourning for his birth mother, Lady Peng.
s0042.idiomatic: In year 11 he left office to mourn his birth mother, Lady Peng.

s0043.literal: Before long he was recalled as central guard general; credential staff, command, and inspectorate were unchanged.
s0043.idiomatic: Soon he was recalled as central guard general with the same credential staff, command, and inspectorate.

s0044.literal: In Jin times many lords and nobles were buried at Meiling; when Peng died, Shuling memorialized asking to bury her at Meiling. He then opened the old tomb of Grand Tutor Xie An, cast out An's coffin, and buried his mother there.
s0044.idiomatic: In Jin many nobles were buried at Meiling; when Peng died Shuling asked to bury her there, opened Grand Tutor Xie An's old tomb, cast out An's coffin, and laid his mother in the grave.

s0045.literal: On the first day of mourning he feigned grief and ruin, claiming he pricked his blood to copy the Nirvana Sutra; before ten days had passed he ordered the kitchen to slaughter fresh meat and daily sent rich delicacies.
s0045.idiomatic: On the first day of mourning he faked grief, claiming he copied the Nirvana Sutra in his own blood; within ten days he had the kitchen serve fresh slaughter and daily delicacies.

s0046.literal: He also secretly summoned the wives and daughters of his attendants and fornicated with them; his conduct was especially beyond the bounds, and the offense reached the emperor's ears.
s0046.idiomatic: He secretly summoned attendants' wives and daughters and lay with them; his conduct was utterly lawless, and word reached the throne.

s0047.literal: Emperor Gaozong reprimanded censor-in-chief Wang Zheng for failing to memorialize and report, removed Zheng from office, also dismissed his recorder and personal attendant, and still added flogging.
s0047.idiomatic: Emperor Gaozong rebuked censor-in-chief Wang Zheng for not reporting him, stripped Zheng of office, dismissed his recorder and personal staff, and had them flogged besides.

s0048.literal: Emperor Gaozong had long loved Shuling and did not bind him with law, but only reproved him.
s0048.idiomatic: Emperor Gaozong had long favored Shuling and would not restrain him by law, only scold him.

s0049.literal: When mourning ended, he again became palace attendant and grand general of the central army.
s0049.idiomatic: When mourning ended he again became palace attendant and grand general of the central army.

s0050.literal: When Emperor Gaozong fell ill, the crown prince and all the princes entered to attend the sickness.
s0050.idiomatic: When Emperor Gaozong fell ill, the crown prince and all princes came in to attend him.

s0051.literal: Emperor Gaozong died in the Hall of Extending Blessings; on the morrow at dawn, as the Last Ruler in grief collapsed prostrate, Shuling with a medicine-grinding knife hacked the Last Ruler in the nape of the neck.
s0051.idiomatic: Emperor Gaozong died in the Hall of Extending Blessings; at dawn the next day, as the Last Ruler lay prostrate in grief, Shuling struck him in the back of the neck with a medicine knife.

s0052.literal: The empress dowager rushed to save him; Shuling also hacked the empress dowager several times.
s0052.idiomatic: The empress dowager rushed to save him; Shuling hacked her several times as well.

s0053.literal: The Last Ruler's wet nurse, Lady Wu, was then at the empress dowager's side; from behind she pulled his elbow, and the Last Ruler was thereby able to rise.
s0053.idiomatic: The Last Ruler's wet nurse, Lady Wu, stood beside the empress dowager and pulled his elbow from behind, so the Last Ruler was able to rise.

s0054.literal: Shuling still held the Last Ruler's garment; the Last Ruler by struggling broke free.
s0054.idiomatic: Shuling still clutched the Last Ruler's robe, but the Last Ruler wrenched free.

s0055.literal: Prince of Changsha Chen Shujian seized Shuling by hand, wrested away his knife, and still dragged him to a pillar and bound him with the sleeve of his robe.
s0055.idiomatic: Prince of Changsha Chen Shujian grappled Shuling, snatched away his knife, dragged him to a pillar, and bound him with his own robe sleeve.

s0056.literal: By then Lady Wu had already helped the Last Ruler flee the assailant; Shujian sought where the Last Ruler was, intending to receive his command.
s0056.idiomatic: By then Lady Wu had helped the Last Ruler escape; Shujian looked for the Last Ruler to receive orders.

s0057.literal: Shuling then by flinging his sleeve broke free, burst out through the Cloud Dragon Gate, galloped in his carriage back to the Eastern Mansion, called up his armored men, scattered gold and silver as reward, and summoned the princes and generals from outside—but none responded except Prince of Xin'an Chen Bogu, who on hearing came to join him.
s0057.idiomatic: Shuling shook free his sleeve, bolted out the Cloud Dragon Gate, raced to the Eastern Mansion, rallied his guards, scattered gold and silver as bounty, and called the princes and generals—but only Prince of Xin'an Chen Bogu came when he heard.

s0058.literal: Shuling gathered troops of barely a thousand; at first he intended to hold the city and defend, but soon right guard general Xiao Mohe led troops to the western gate of the mansion; Shuling, the affair urgent, in panic and fear sent recorder Wei Liang to present his pipes and drums to Mohe, and still told him: "If the affair succeeds, you will certainly be made one of the highest ministers."
s0058.idiomatic: Shuling mustered barely a thousand men and at first meant to hold the city, but right guard Xiao Mohe soon brought troops to the mansion's western gate. In panic Shuling sent staff recorder Wei Liang with his pipes and drums and promised, "If we win, you will sit among the highest ministers."

s0059.literal: Mohe deceived him in reply, saying, "I must wait until Your Highness's trusted backbone commanders come in person before I dare obey the command."
s0059.idiomatic: Mohe lied in answer: "I must wait until Your Highness's own trusted commanders come before I dare obey."

s0060.literal: Shuling at once sent Dai Wen and Tan Qilin, two men, to Mohe's camp; Mohe seized them and sent them to the tribunal; they were beheaded beneath the covered way.
s0060.idiomatic: Shuling sent Dai Wen and Tan Qilin to Mohe's camp; Mohe seized them, sent them to the tribunal, and they were beheaded under the gallery.

s0061.literal: Shuling knew himself beyond saving; he then entered the inner quarters and drowned his consort Lady Zhang and seven favored concubines in a well.
s0061.idiomatic: Knowing all was lost, Shuling went inside and drowned his consort Lady Zhang and seven favored concubines in a well.

s0062.literal: Shuling had subordinate troops earlier at Xinlin; he then led several hundred horse and foot, crossed from the small ferry, and intended to hurry to Xinlin and enter the north by warship.
s0062.idiomatic: Some of his men were already at Xinlin; he led several hundred horse and foot across the small ferry, meaning to reach Xinlin and flee north by ship.

s0063.literal: When they reached Baiyang Road they were intercepted by the court army; Bogu, seeing troops arrive, at once dodged into a lane; Shuling spurred his horse, drew his blade, and pursued; Bogu came back again.
s0063.idiomatic: At Baiyang Road the court army blocked them; Bogu, seeing soldiers, slipped into an alley; Shuling spurred after him with blade drawn, and Bogu returned.

s0064.literal: Shuling's followers for the most part cast off armor and scattered; Mohe's horse
s0064.idiomatic: Shuling's men mostly threw off armor and fled; Mohe on horseback

s0066.literal: Collation variant: (Rong); adopted reading: Chen Zhishen came forward to stab Shuling. Editorial footnote marker 1. He stiffened and fell dead on the ground; the eunuch Wang Feiqin drew his blade and hacked him more than ten times; horse
s0066.idiomatic: Collation variant: (Rong); adopted reading: Chen Zhishen came forward to stab Shuling. [1] He stiffened and fell dead; the eunuch Wang Feiqin drew his blade and hacked him more than ten times; on horseback

s0068.literal: Collation variant: (Rong); adopted reading: Chen Zhonghua then cut off his head and sent it to the tribunal.
s0068.idiomatic: Collation variant: (Rong); adopted reading: Chen Zhonghua then cut off his head and sent it to the tribunal.

s0069.literal: From the hour yin to the hour si order was restored.
s0069.idiomatic: From dawn till mid-morning order was restored.

s0070.literal: The eight seats of the Secretariat memorialized: "The rebel traitor, the late palace attendant and grand general of the central army, Prince of Shixing Chen Shuling, was perverse in youth and in age indulged greed and cruelty.
s0070.idiomatic: The eight secretariat ministers memorialized: "The traitor, the late palace attendant and grand general of the central army, Prince of Shixing Chen Shuling, was savage from childhood and in manhood wallowed in greed and cruelty.

s0071.literal: Sent out to pacify south of Xiang and when he held the Nine Waters, in both jurisdictions the common people were swept clean, none left.
s0071.idiomatic: As governor south of Xiang and later on the Nine Waters, he left both regions' common folk swept bare.

s0072.literal: Bee eyes and jackal voice, intimate with the frivolous; unfilial and unkind, he relied on arms and was cruel by nature; without rites and without righteousness—only slaughter was heard of him.
s0072.idiomatic: With bee eyes and jackal voice he consorted with the worthless; unfilial, unkind, he trusted to arms and delighted in cruelty; without rite or right, only killing followed his name.

s0073.literal: When he dwelt in partial mourning, he gave himself to lust and pleasure; sons born, he lodged them in guest houses—day and night in succession.
s0073.idiomatic: During his mother's mourning he abandoned himself to lust; when sons were born he lodged them in guest quarters, one birth after another without pause.

s0074.literal: By day he hid, by night he roamed, constantly practicing treachery and deceit, plundering the people, repeatedly opening tombs.
s0074.idiomatic: He hid by day and prowled by night, ever scheming, plundering townsfolk and opening grave after grave.

s0075.literal: Grand Tutor Xie aided Jin in founding the mandate and helped create the southeast; to chop open the coffin and expose the bones shocked every ear and eye.
s0075.idiomatic: Grand Tutor Xie had aided Jin in founding the realm and shaping the southeast; to break open his coffin and bare his bones horrified all who heard.

s0076.literal: From the time the late emperor took to his sickbed, on the morrow he did not recover; Shuling, in a position of high honor, attended the medicines—outwardly without grief, inwardly harboring regicide.
s0076.idiomatic: From the day the late emperor fell ill, by the morrow he had not recovered; Shuling, in honored rank at the bedside, showed no sorrow outwardly while nursing regicide within.

s0077.literal: After the final decline, as the sacred person wailed and beat his breast, he took advantage of prostration and with his hand violated the imperial carriage.
s0077.idiomatic: When the emperor was failing, as the sacred person wailed and beat his breast, Shuling used the prostration to lay hands on the imperial person.

s0078.literal: When the empress dowager came in person, he again added the blade; utterly vicious, extreme in treason—unmatched since antiquity.
s0078.idiomatic: When the empress dowager came in person he struck her again; such extreme villainy had no parallel in antiquity.

s0079.literal: Thanks to Prince of Changsha Chen Shujian, whose filial devotion was earnest to the utmost and whose heroic resolve flared up, who with his hands seized and crushed him and with his body shielded the sacred person.
s0079.idiomatic: Only Prince of Changsha Chen Shujian, utterly earnest in loyalty, seized him with his own hands and shielded the emperor with his body.

s0080.literal: Shuling still fled to the eastern city, gathered vicious partisans—the poison not yet spent—and killed his wife and children himself.
s0080.idiomatic: Shuling still fled to the eastern quarter, rallied his ruffians, and even murdered his own wife and children.

s0081.literal: Though in due time he was beheaded and hung up, our indignant grief is not yet vented; we your subjects jointly deliberate and ask, following the Song dynasty precedent, to float the corpse in the middle of the river, befoul his dwelling with filth, and also destroy the tombs and temples of his birth mother Lady Peng and restore the mound of the Xie clan."
s0081.idiomatic: Though he was promptly beheaded, our rage is not spent. We jointly ask, as in Song precedent, to cast his corpse into mid-river, befoul his house, destroy his mother Lady Peng's tomb and shrine, and restore the Xie burial mound."

s0082.literal: " The edict said: "The vicious traitor, owl and cur, turned to bite the palace apartments; thanks to the imperial ancestors' spirits, he was quickly cut down.
s0082.idiomatic: "The edict read: "The traitor, more beast than man, turned to savage the inner palace; thanks to the imperial ancestors' spirits he was swiftly destroyed.

s0083.literal: Editorial footnote marker 2. When I consider the matter with feeling and speak to the facts, bitterness and indignation are both in my breast; the court deliberation has proper regulations—it is fitting to follow what was memorialized."
s0083.idiomatic: [2] Considering the matter in grief and speaking to the facts, bitterness and indignation fill my breast; the court's deliberation is in order, and it is fitting to follow what was memorialized."

s0084.literal: Shuling's sons, that same day, were all granted death.
s0084.idiomatic: Shuling's sons were all ordered to die that same day.

s0085.literal: Former Hengyang inner administrator Peng Hao, deliberation staff officer and concurrent recorder Zheng Xin, central recorder staff officer and concurrent recorder Wei Liang, and recorder Yu Gongxi were all executed.
s0085.idiomatic: Former Hengyang inner administrator Peng Hao, deliberation officer and recorder Zheng Xin, central recorder and recorder Wei Liang, and recorder Yu Gongxi were all put to death.

s0086.literal: Hao was Shuling's maternal uncle; he had early followed Emperor Gaozong in Guanzhong and had considerable merit, and through Shuling's patronage commanded troops and held Liyang and Hengyang, two commanderies.
s0086.idiomatic: Hao was Shuling's uncle on his mother's side; he had followed Emperor Gaozong in Guanzhong with some merit and, through Shuling's favor, held command over Liyang and Hengyang.

s0087.literal: Xin, because he was skilled in shorthand, was favored; in planning and counsel he had a part in everything.
s0087.idiomatic: Xin was skilled at shorthand and enjoyed favor; he took part in every plan.

s0088.literal: Liang was a native of Jingzhao, son of Liang attendant-in-ordinary and protector-general Can; he was brought in by Shuling for his learning.
s0088.idiomatic: Liang came from Jingzhao, son of Liang attendant-in-ordinary and protector-general Can, and was recruited by Shuling for his scholarship.

s0089.literal: Chen Zhishen, for merit in executing Shuling, was made inner administrator of Baling and enfeoffed as Viscount of You'an.
s0089.idiomatic: For killing Shuling, Chen Zhishen was made inner administrator of Baling and enfeoffed as Viscount of You'an.

s0090.literal: Chen Zhonghua was made administrator of Xia Gui and enfeoffed as Viscount of Xinyi.
s0090.idiomatic: Chen Zhonghua was made administrator of Xia Gui and enfeoffed as Viscount of Xinyi.

s0091.literal: Wang Feiqin was appointed general who crosses the waves.
s0091.idiomatic: Wang Feiqin was made general who crosses the waves.

s0092.literal: Editorial footnote marker 3. Gold was bestowed to each in differing amounts.
s0092.idiomatic: [3] Gold was bestowed in differing amounts to each.

s0094.literal: Prince of Xin'an Chen Bogu, styled Laozhi, was the fifth son of Emperor Wen.
s0094.idiomatic: Prince of Xin'an Chen Bogu, styled Laozhi, was Emperor Wen's fifth son.

s0095.literal: From birth he had a pigeon chest; his eyes were clear with the whites showing; his form was slight and small, yet he was handsome in debate and skilled in discourse.
s0095.idiomatic: He was born with a pigeon chest and eyes whose whites showed bright; though slight in stature he was handsome in debate and fluent in speech.

s0096.literal: In the sixth year of Tianchen, he was established as Prince of Xin'an with a fief of two thousand households.
s0096.idiomatic: In Tianchen year 6 he was made Prince of Xin'an with a fief of two thousand households.

s0097.literal: When the Deposed Emperor succeeded, he was made credential-bearing, commander of all military affairs in southern Langye, Pengcheng, and Donghai, cloud-banner general, and administrator of Pengcheng and Langye.
s0097.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor succeeded, he received the credential staff, command of southern Langye, Pengcheng, and Donghai, the rank of cloud-banner general, and the Pengcheng and Langye administratorates.

s0098.literal: Soon he entered court as governor of Danyang; his general's rank was unchanged.
s0098.idiomatic: Soon he entered court as governor of Danyang, keeping his general's rank.

s0099.literal: In the first year of Taijian, he was advanced to general of intelligent martiality; his governorship was unchanged.
s0099.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 he was promoted to general of intelligent martiality while keeping the Danyang post.

s0100.literal: When his term ended, he was advanced to general who assists the right.
s0100.idiomatic: When his term expired he was promoted to general who assists the right.
